New York City’s public schools will temporarily ban elementary and middle school students from using generative artificial intelligence tools during the upcoming school year, Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Wednesday.
As we prepare to welcome students back to school on September 10, I am writing to share details on our 2026–2027 artificial intelligence (AI) and screen time policy for NYC Public Schools (NYCPS).
The student-facing restrictions described on this page apply specifically to generative AI.

Five pilots have been centrally approved for grades 9–12 (Quill, Edia, Brisk Teaching, Playlab, and Intel AI-Ready Schools). Any high school may apply for any of the five pilots, and each application will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. Regarding individual student exposure to AI, we will ensure that students are participating in only one pilot.

Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and Schools Chancellor Kamar H. Samuels today announced a moratorium on student-facing generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) use in schools, alongside a new screen time policy, a decision that will impact nearly 600,000 public school students, or two-thirds of the system’s total enrollment. The policy establishes a one-year moratorium, effective in the 2026-2027 school year, on student-facing generative AI for children in 2-K through 8th grade. It also introduces twice-yearly AI critical thinking modules for high schoolers, limited AI pilots for a small number of high school classrooms and age-appropriate screen time restrictions.

Across all grades, this policy does not apply to assistive technology and associated screen time, provided through a student's Individualized Education Plan (IEP) or 504 Plan. Students with disabilities and English Language Learners (ELLs) will continue to have access to other necessary tools.

For the 2026-27 school year, New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) is implementing a moratorium on student-facing generative artificial intelligence (AI) in grades 2K–8, with limited use in high schools, and screen time restrictions depending on grade.

Teachers and other school staff members may continue using AI for instructional planning and operational tasks, subject to existing requirements, including the NYCPS Enterprise Request Management Application (ERMA) data privacy and security approval process, and NYCPS procurement rules. Additionally, AI may not be used for grading, behavior monitoring, or for placement, promotion, graduation, and other decisions about students. All special education documents are developed by qualified professionals; counseling, crisis intervention, and therapeutic support are provided only by qualified staff members.

Michael Mulgrew, president of the United Federation of Teachers in New York, praised the screen time limits but said the city’s AI policy “leaves many questions unanswered,” including how the Education Department “will be more aggressive in demanding the products it purchases have AI safeguards.”

Josh Golin, executive director of the children’s advocacy group Fairplay, said he would have preferred a longer moratorium and more time between the announcement and the start of the school year. “A year to evaluate is not nearly enough time,” he said, adding that the onus should be on AI platforms “to demonstrate that their products are effective at teaching kids, that they’re safe, that they’re not displacing face-to-face interaction and that they’re not leading to rampant cheating.”

For AI tools being used in your child's school, contact your school principal. For concerns, you can contact your child's school, the School Leadership Team (SLT) or your Community Education Council (CEC).

While public feedback survey is now closed, you can share feedback directly to your school, participate in your school's PTA, attend your local Community Education Council events, or the Panel for Educational Policy.

The Technology in Schools Coalition, comprised of students, educators, parent leaders, elected officials, advocates, union partners, and experts in the field, will provide recommendations on the future of technology use in NYCPS classrooms and will deliver a report of policy recommendations in April 2027.
